analyst:
Houston enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 28-6 overall and 14-4 in the Big 12 after reaching the Big 12 Tournament title game and losing 79-74 to Arizona on March 14. ESPN’s schedule page lists Houston as 28-6 and second in the Big 12, and Sports-Reference’s school index shows the Cougars finished the regular season 26-5 with a 14-4 league mark before conference tournament play. Their NCAA opener is listed for Thursday, March 19, 2026, against Idaho. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/248/season/2026))

Offensively, this is still a Kelvin Sampson team in the traditional sense: guard-driven, half-court physical, and built on paint touches leading to kick-out threes or offensive-rebound chances. The numbers back that up. Through Feb. 24, Houston averaged 76.6 points per game, shot 44.4% from the field, attempted 730 threes in 28 games, and posted 36.9 rebounds per game with 368 offensive boards; that offensive rebounding volume is central to how they create second possessions. Their assist leaders also tell the story of a ball-screen and drive-and-kick attack: Kingston Flemings had 143 assists in 28 games, Milos Uzan 113, and Emanuel Sharp spaced the floor with 75 made threes. Houston’s late-game shot profile repeatedly ran through those guards. In the Jan. 6 win over Texas Tech, Flemings scored nine points in the final two minutes of a 69-65 win, showing Sampson’s preference to flatten the floor and trust his lead guard to create. In the Nov. 24 overtime win over Syracuse, Uzan and Sharp scored all 11 Houston points in OT of a 78-74 win, another example of the Cougars defaulting to experienced guard creation when possessions tighten. Scheme-wise, outside observers and coaching breakdowns have consistently identified Sampson’s offense with pick-and-roll, floppy action for shooters, and strong BLOB/ATO execution, and Houston’s personnel usage this season fits that description exactly: Uzan and Flemings initiate, Sharp works as the primary movement shooter, and Chris Cenac Jr. and Joseph Tugler function as screeners, rollers, and second-chance finishers. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/season_stats__pdf_.pdf))

Defensively, Houston remains one of the clearest identity teams in the field. The raw numbers are blunt: opponents were held to 62.3 points per game, 40.0% shooting overall, and 31.6% from three through Feb. 24, while Houston forced 388 turnovers in 28 games and recorded 217 steals plus 108 blocks. Tugler is the tone-setter on the front line with 41 blocks and 37 steals through 28 games, and a Houston preview noted he was averaging 2.0 steals and 1.7 blocks per game in January, making him one of the few Big 12 players ranking near the top of both categories. Philosophically, Sampson’s defense is still aggressive man-to-man built around ball pressure, denial, and hard ball-screen coverage. Opponent scouting from Florida’s 2025 title-game prep explicitly described Houston’s “ball-screen blitz barrage,” and independent tactical breakdowns have described the Cougars as a team that blitzes ball screens, traps corners and post entries, and rarely relies on zone. That profile matches the game outcomes this year: Baylor scored only 64 in Houston’s March 4 comeback win, Kansas managed 47 in the Big 12 Tournament semifinal on March 13, and Utah was held to 52 on Feb. 10. When Houston is dictating, the ball sticks, the dribble gets turned, and the possession ends in a rushed jumper over length. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/season_stats__pdf_.pdf))

Sampson’s coaching philosophy is visible in the way Houston responds inside games and between games. The best recent adjustment example is March 4 against Baylor: Houston trailed before using what the school recap called a “big second-half run” to win 77-64 on Senior Night, with Kingston Flemings scoring 21 and adding seven assists. Another documented pattern is post-loss response. Houston’s Feb. 20 game notes stated that under Sampson the Cougars were 33-2 in games following a regular-season loss since Feb. 1, 2017, and had not lost consecutive games since January 2024. That matters because after the Feb. 23 loss at Kansas, Houston answered with a 102-62 demolition of Colorado on Feb. 28, then beat Baylor 77-64 on March 4 and Oklahoma State 82-75 on March 7. Even specific end-of-game design is part of his résumé: Houston won the 2025 Sweet 16 over Purdue on a sideline out-of-bounds action that produced a game-winning layup, and in the 2025 Final Four Sampson inserted defensive specialist Mylik Wilson after a timeout to disrupt Duke’s inbounds play, a change that directly fed Houston’s comeback win. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/news/2026/3/5/mens-basketball-7-6-mens-basketball-beats-baylor-on-senior-night.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is a real selling point for Houston, but it is not flawless. Best examples: on Nov. 16, Houston beat Auburn 73-72 on a neutral floor, a one-possession result against a top opponent that showed they could close a physical game. On Nov. 24, they beat Syracuse 78-74 in overtime, with Uzan and Sharp combining for all 11 OT points. On Jan. 6, they beat Texas Tech 69-65, with Flemings scoring nine points in the final two minutes. On the other side, Houston’s losses also reveal pressure points. They lost 76-73 to Tennessee on Nov. 25, 70-67 at Iowa State on Feb. 16, and 79-74 to Arizona in the Big 12 Tournament final on March 14. Those games suggest that when Houston cannot fully control tempo, the offense can become more guard-dependent and less efficient late. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/248/season/2026))

The key players start with freshman point guard Kingston Flemings, the engine of the team. Through 28 games he averaged 16.6 points and 5.1 assists, and Houston’s March 9 postseason-awards release listed him at 16.5 points, 5.4 assists, and 1.5 steals per game while shooting 48.3% from the field and 37.6% from three. His standout moments are everywhere: 42 points at Texas Tech on Jan. 24, a school freshman single-game scoring record; 27 at TCU on Jan. 28; 26 points and eight assists were logged by Uzan, not Flemings, in the Colorado win, but Flemings still had eight assists; and he had 21 points and seven assists vs Baylor on March 4. Emanuel Sharp is the primary perimeter scorer and shot-maker, averaging 16.0 points through 28 games with 75 made threes; he scored 27 against Florida State on Dec. 6, 27 at Utah on Feb. 10, and 23 against Kansas State on Feb. 14. Milos Uzan is the second organizer, averaging 11.0 points and 113 assists through 28 games; his biggest games include 26 points vs Syracuse, 26 vs Colorado, and 17 vs West Virginia. Chris Cenac Jr. gives Houston interior scoring and glass work at 9.5 points and 7.8 rebounds per game, with 14 rebounds in the March 13 Big 12 Tournament win over Kansas. Joseph Tugler is the defensive anchor and utility big: 7.5 points, 5.3 rebounds, 41 blocks, 37 steals through 28 games, plus notable lines like 20 points and 10 rebounds in the March 14 loss to Arizona and 11 rebounds at Baylor on Jan. 10. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/season_stats__pdf_.pdf))

The notable wins are high-end and revealing. Auburn, 73-72 on Nov. 16, showed Houston could beat elite athleticism in a grinder. Syracuse, 78-74 in OT on Nov. 24, showed late-game shot creation. Arkansas, 94-85 on Dec. 20, showed this roster has more offensive punch than some prior Sampson teams. Texas Tech, 69-65 on Jan. 6, was a classic control-the-last-four-minutes win. Baylor, 77-64 on March 4, showed second-half adjustment power. Kansas, 69-47 on March 13 in the Big 12 Tournament, showed Houston’s defense at full force. The notable losses are equally informative. Tennessee’s 76-73 win on Nov. 25 exposed some half-court execution issues against comparable physicality. Texas Tech’s 90-86 win on Jan. 24 proved Houston can be dragged into a higher-possession shootout. Iowa State’s 70-67 win on Feb. 16 and Arizona’s 73-66 win on Feb. 21 came during Houston’s worst stretch of the season, and Kansas finished the regular-season upset with a 69-56 result on Feb. 23. That three-loss stretch, followed immediately by a 102-62 win over Colorado, is probably the clearest evidence of both Houston’s vulnerability and its ceiling. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/248/season/2026))

As for tournament pedigree, Sampson brings one of the strongest March résumés in the field. Sports-Reference lists him with 21 NCAA Tournament appearances, a 31-21 NCAA record, and three Final Fours. Houston’s official bio says he led Oklahoma to the 2002 Final Four and 2003 Elite Eight, and at Houston he has taken the Cougars to the 2021 Final Four and the 2025 national championship game. In year-by-year round terms, his deepest documented runs are: 2002 Final Four with Oklahoma, 2003 Elite Eight with Oklahoma, 2021 Final Four with Houston, 2022 Elite Eight with Houston, and 2025 national runner-up with Houston after reaching the title game. That history matters because Houston does not have to guess what this month should look like under pressure: Sampson has already coached teams to the second weekend repeatedly and to the final weekend three different times. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/coaches/kelvin-sampson-1.html?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Houston is a veteran-coached, defense-first contender with enough perimeter creation to win ugly or efficient games. The exact profile is 28-6, 14-4 Big 12, 76.6 points scored and 62.3 allowed through the key late-February statistical checkpoint, with Flemings, Sharp, Uzan, Tugler, and Cenac giving Sampson his usual blend of toughness plus more shot-making than some of his earlier Houston teams. If the Cougars get the game into the half court and make opponents play through bodies and traps for 40 minutes, they look like a second-weekend team at minimum; if the offense bogs down into pure bailout ball, the close losses to Tennessee, Iowa State, Kansas, and Arizona show the risk. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/24/season_stats__pdf_.pdf))
forecaster:
Houston enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with the profile of a true national-title-caliber team: elite by every major predictive system, battle-tested by a strong Big 12 schedule, and still built in the Kelvin Sampson mold around defense, physicality, and offensive glass pressure. WarrenNolan’s 2026 team sheet lists Houston at 28-6 against Division I competition, 14-4 in the Big 12, with a NET ranking of No. 5. That same sheet also shows Houston at No. 4 in ESPN’s BPI, No. 5 in KenPom/Pomeroy, and No. 5 in Bart Torvik’s T-Rank. In other words, across the committee-facing and predictive ecosystems, Houston is not merely “good enough for a protected seed”; it is clustered firmly in the top tier of the sport. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Houston))

The schedule profile is strong, though not maximally punishing in the non-conference. WarrenNolan lists Houston’s overall NET strength of schedule at No. 24 nationally, with a non-conference NET SOS of No. 113. Its RPI-based SOS sits at No. 21, with a non-conference RPI SOS of No. 187. That combination matters analytically: Houston did not build this résumé solely by overwhelming a brutal November and December slate, but by surviving and largely thriving in a high-end conference environment. The team sheet also shows a 12-1 Division I non-conference record and average opponent NETs of 102 in wins and 12 in losses, which suggests the losses came almost entirely against top-shelf competition rather than to mid-tier teams. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Houston))

On pure ranking consensus, Houston looks slightly stronger in résumé metrics than casual perception might assume. ESPN’s 2025-26 BPI overview page places Houston third nationally overall, behind only Duke and Michigan. ESPN’s resume view places Houston ninth, while WarrenNolan’s team sheet has BPI at No. 4 and NET at No. 5. Bart Torvik’s searchable 2026 T-Rank output also places Houston fifth nationally. The broad takeaway is that Houston is not just a defense-first grinder surviving close games; the computers see a complete team with a top-five to top-three national ceiling depending on model flavor. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi/_/view/overview/group/50))

Offensively, the public-facing data that is actually accessible points to a unit better than the stereotype. ESPN’s offense-sorted BPI page places Houston 12th nationally in offensive strength. That is an important corrective to conventional wisdom. Houston is still thought of primarily as a bruising half-court defensive machine, but top-12 offensive strength in BPI means the attack is materially better than the old “just enough scoring” Houston versions. This aligns with what observers have seen from the Cougars over the last two seasons: more perimeter shot-making, better guard orchestration, and enough creation to avoid being purely dependent on second chances. If the eye test says “defense-first,” the numbers say “defense-first, but with a genuinely high-level offense attached.” ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi/_/sort/bpi.bpioffense/dir/desc))

Defensively, even without every exact possession-based split being publicly exposed in accessible sources, the profile remains unmistakable. Houston’s No. 5 KenPom rank, No. 5 Torvik rank, and No. 5 NET alongside a 28-6 record in the Big 12 strongly imply the defense is once again carrying an elite efficiency base. Recent game-level data from Sports-Reference reinforces that. In a February 4 win over UCF, Houston posted a 125.4 offensive rating and allowed just 87.3, a massive per-100-possession margin. In a November neutral-site win over Notre Dame, Houston recorded a 104.8 offensive rating, 89.0 defensive rating, and a 63.0-possession game, which is classic Houston territory: controlled tempo, suppressed opponent efficiency, and enough shot quality to win comfortably. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2026-02-04-01-houston.html?utm_source=openai))

Tempo remains an important part of the story. The available game logs point to Houston playing many games in the low-60s possession range; the Notre Dame example was exactly 63.0 possessions. That is consistent with Sampson-era Houston generally preferring a measured pace rather than a track meet. So while I could not verify a single season-long possessions-per-40 figure from an accessible primary page, the evidence strongly supports the conclusion that Houston is still relatively slow by national-contender standards. That slow pace can distort eye-test evaluations: because games are compressed, Houston can look less explosive than it actually is. But efficiency models are specifically designed to correct for pace, and those models still rate the Cougars as top-five nationally. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/houston/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

The most Houston-specific fingerprint, as usual, is likely in the possession battle categories: turnover avoidance, offensive rebounding, and physical shot contesting. Exact season-long team values for eFG%, TO%, OR%, FT rate, and 3-point attempt rate were not fully accessible in open sources during this search, but game-level evidence and the long-running Sampson blueprint suggest Houston is winning with an unusual combination of defensive resistance and possession leverage. The UCF advanced box showed Houston with an offensive rebounding rate of 41.4% in that game and a turnover rate of just 11.1%, while forcing UCF into a 16.8% turnover rate. That single-game snapshot is not a season average, but it is highly illustrative of the team’s style: end possessions cleanly on defense, extend them on offense, and avoid giving the ball away. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/boxscores/2026-02-04-01-houston.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent form also looks strong overall, even with a few reminders of vulnerability. NCAA.com noted on January 24 that Houston was 17-2, 5-1 in the Big 12, had won 11 straight, and owned the nation’s longest road winning streak at 16 before a loss at Texas Tech. On February 21, NCAA.com reported a home loss to Iowa State, 73-66, handing Houston a rare defeat in its own building. By late February, Sports-Reference box-score indexing showed Houston at 24-5 before a win over Colorado, and WarrenNolan’s current team sheet now lists the Cougars at 28-6. That trajectory suggests a team that took some hits in February but still closed the pre-tournament stretch with enough consistency to remain top-five in the key systems. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2026-01-24/texas-tech-north-carolina-mens-basketball-deliver-big-wins-top-25-showdowns?utm_source=openai))

So where do the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom? First, Houston’s offense appears materially stronger than its reputation; a top-12 BPI offense is not the profile of a one-dimensional grinder. Second, the non-conference schedule was decent rather than brutal, but the overall résumé still rates like a top-five team because the Big 12 work was so strong. Third, the likely slow pace can make Houston seem less dominant possession to possession than it actually is; efficiency models smooth that out and still love the Cougars. The most coherent analytical summary is this: Houston is still unmistakably Houston in style, but this version is less dependent on ugly-game variance than earlier editions. The defense and rebounding identity remain the anchor, yet the national metrics indicate an offense good enough to support a title run rather than merely avoid sabotaging one. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi/_/sort/bpi.bpioffense/dir/desc))
matchup-analyst:
Houston is still a Kelvin Sampson team first: low-possession, half-court control, elite ball security, hard-nosed point-of-attack defense, and constant second-effort pressure on the glass. Through Selection Sunday, Houston was 28-6, ranked No. 5 in NET and No. 6 by RotoWire’s team page, scoring 77.6 points per game while allowing 62.7. Their offensive rating was 119.1 at Sports-Reference and 1.23 points per possession at RotoWire, while their pace was only 64.7 possessions per game, 358th nationally. That means Houston is most comfortable turning games into 64-66 possession grinders, not races. If you let them dictate tempo, you are playing their game. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/houston/men/2026-gamelogs.html?utm_source=openai))

The core style is clear in the numbers and personnel. Houston protects the ball exceptionally well: 8.2 turnovers per game in the official team stats through Feb. 14, and a 10.96% turnover rate at RotoWire, third nationally. Kingston Flemings is the engine, averaging 16.4 points and 5.3 assists per game on the season; Emanuel Sharp adds 16.6 points and 68 made threes through Feb. 14; Milos Uzan gives them another decision-maker with 101 assists against 35 turnovers through that same official stat packet. Houston wants multiple handlers on the floor, few live-ball mistakes, and then to win the possession battle with offensive rebounding and defensive turnovers. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/14/Season_Stats__PDF_.pdf))

Specific tactics that disrupt Houston: switchable length on the perimeter, physical defensive rebounding, and forcing them to finish over size without bailout second chances. The best example is Kansas on Feb. 23: Houston scored only 56 points in a 69-56 loss on 65 possessions, good for an 86.3 offensive rating. Houston shot 21-for-66 overall, 5-for-24 from three, and had an eFG% of .356. Kansas also held them to 10 offensive rebounds total and just a .136 free-throw rate. Named matchup example: Kansas wings Tre White and Darryn Peterson combined for 37 points, while Houston’s primary creators struggled — Sharp went 1-for-10, Uzan 3-for-7, and Flemings 6-for-18. That is the blueprint: long guards crowd the catch, stay attached to shooters, and make Houston win with contested two-point finishing. ([basketball.realgm.com](https://basketball.realgm.com/ncaa/boxscore/2026-02-23/Houston-at-Kansas/510448))

Press vulnerability is limited in the traditional sense because Houston almost never beats itself with turnovers. Iowa State, one of the country’s best pressure teams, beat Houston 70-67 on Feb. 16, but even in defeat Houston still only committed three turnovers — tied for the Big 12 conference low allowed by Iowa State’s opponents. So full-court pressure by itself is not the answer. The better lesson from Iowa State is to use pressure to drain clock, flatten Houston’s spacing, and make them initiate offense late. Even when they survive the press, you shorten the usable half-court window. Iowa State won despite Houston’s ball security because the game stayed in the mud and the Cyclones closed on a 17-4 run, per FOX’s recap. ([foxsports.com](https://www.foxsports.com/college-basketball/houston-cougars-vs-iowa-state-cyclones-feb-16-2026-game-boxscore-262794?utm_source=openai))

Zone vulnerability is more plausible than press vulnerability, but the evidence says it must be a selective changeup, not a base defense. Houston’s offense is only 141st nationally in effective FG% at 52.10 despite elite turnover avoidance, which means if you remove their clean catch-and-shoot rhythm and finish possessions with rebounds, their shot-making can wobble. Kansas is the best example of that wobble, and Arizona also did it in a 73-66 win at Houston on Feb. 21; Arizona led by as many as 10 in the first half and held Houston to 66 points. The inference here is that Houston’s offense is more execution-driven than isolation-proof: if your zone has length on the wings and quick closeouts to Sharp/Uzan, you can make them settle. But if your zone cannot rebound, Houston will shred it with second shots because its offensive rebounding rate is 35.89%, 29th nationally. ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/houston-1436))

Preferred pace is slow; the way to force the opposite is to score before Houston sets its shell and to attack misses and makes alike with early drag screens and rim runs. Texas Tech’s 90-86 win on Jan. 24 is the clearest case. That game exploded beyond Houston’s comfort zone: Tech scored 55 first-half points, the most Houston had allowed in any half of the Sampson era according to ESPN Research via the game reaction cited in search results. Texas Tech hit 12 threes, won the rebound battle 44-28, grabbed 18 offensive rebounds, and got 31 points from JT Toppin. If you can make Houston play an 80-plus-possession feel game — or at least a game with frequent early-clock actions and cross-matches — you pull them away from their preferred control environment. ([thescore.com](https://www.thescore.com/ncaab/events/2458051/box_score))

Position-by-position mismatches: at point guard, Flemings is strong and poised but only 6-4; bigger lead guards who can see over traps and punish switches are useful. Iowa State and Kansas both won with bigger, physical perimeter groups. At the two, Sharp is 6-3 and 205 pounds, but he is more valuable as a shot-maker than as a downhill creator; making him defend larger wings and then attack him off movement can tax him. At the three, Uzan is listed 6-4 and 195 and often functions as a secondary handler rather than a true wing stopper; big wings like Kansas’ 6-7 Tre White produced 23 points and 8 free throws in that Feb. 23 game. In the frontcourt, Joseph Tugler is disruptive but only 22.3 minutes per game through Feb. 14 because of fouls/usage constraints, while Chris Cenac Jr. is 6-11 and productive but still a freshman. Elite scoring 4s and 5s have had success: JT Toppin’s 31 and 12 for Texas Tech is the best single-game evidence. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster?utm_source=openai))

Houston is not an isolation-heavy offense by profile; it is a team-offense, decision-making, offensive-rebounding offense. The available 2026 primary-source team data does not publish Synergy isolation-usage percentages openly, so I cannot responsibly fabricate exact iso share. What the available stats do show is that Houston averages 15.4 assists per game against only 8.2 turnovers in the official packet, and 1.9 assist/turnover ratio overall, which strongly indicates a pass-and-advantage offense rather than a pure matchup-hunt attack. Their 40.78% 3PA/FGA rate also shows they are willing to play inside-out but not as a rim-pressure-heavy isolation team; their free-throw attempt rate is only 26.92, 352nd nationally. In plain terms: Houston would rather beat you with execution, spacing, and extra possessions than with repeated one-on-one creation. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/14/Season_Stats__PDF_.pdf))

Transition frequency data is not publicly available from the primary sources surfaced here, so exact possession-share percentages for transition offense/defense cannot be stated with confidence. But the tactical evidence is still usable. Houston’s very slow pace, elite ball security, and low turnover rate suppress transition volume overall, while their defensive pressure creates selective runouts. Against Kansas State on Feb. 14, the official box listed Houston with 20 fast-break points; against teams that force them into more open-floor exchanges, their advantage narrows because the game becomes less about set defense and more about athletic recovery. Texas Tech’s Jan. 24 win and Arizona’s Feb. 21 win both pushed Houston into more uncomfortable tempo swings than Houston prefers. ([cyclones.com](https://cyclones.com/documents/download/2026/2/16/26-Houston.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Coaching adaptability: yes, Sampson’s staff is highly adaptive game to game and within games, even if the prompt says “mid-series” and college basketball does not have playoff series. Houston’s 2025 NCAA run is a strong example of in-tournament adjustment. They beat Tennessee 69-50 in the 2025 Elite Eight by turning the game into a defensive chokehold after prior rounds against very different offensive profiles, and they rallied from behind to beat Duke 70-67 in the 2025 national semifinal. In 2026, Houston also rebounded from the Iowa State/Kansas skid by beating Baylor 77-64 on March 4 and then Oklahoma State 82-75 on March 7, with role-player adaptation visible: Chase McCarty scored 20 off the bench vs. Oklahoma State after lineup uncertainty, and Tugler’s offensive role ticked up in March. That is real evidence that the staff will alter rotation emphasis and coverage details quickly. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/b08fb811aa9273ab476804f75f02f6b5?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Houston, you must do five specific things. First, keep the game out of the low-60s in possessions by running after makes and misses and flowing directly into early offense; Texas Tech’s 90 points is the model. Second, put a big scoring forward or center into repeated screening actions against Cenac/Tugler and make Houston’s back line choose between helping on the roll and staying home on shooters; Toppin’s 31-point, 12-rebound game is the template. Third, use pressure as a clock weapon, not a turnover hunt — Iowa State proved Houston will often survive the press but can still be forced deep into possessions. Fourth, crowd Sharp and Uzan off the arc with length and finish the possession with one rebound; Kansas held Houston to 5-for-24 from three and a .356 eFG. Fifth, attack their guards with size: make Tre White-type wings or oversized initiators post, drive, and cut against them until Houston has to send extra help. If you fail to rebound or if you allow Houston’s guards to play clean, two-pass offense into spot-up threes, you will lose the possession battle and probably the game. ([thescore.com](https://www.thescore.com/ncaab/events/2458051/box_score))

One limitation note: exact 2026 Synergy-style percentages for isolation share, transition frequency, and zone-specific possession outcomes were not publicly accessible from primary sources in the search results, so those exact percentage fields could not be verified and are therefore not invented here. The report instead relies on official Houston stat packets, box scores, and credible season-summary sources to stay evidence-based. ([uhcougars.com](https://uhcougars.com/documents/download/2026/2/14/Season_Stats__PDF_.pdf))
